newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Diligentia listing ends Sweden bank property woes.
newsitem.headline: Diligentia listing ends Sweden bank property woes.

text.p: Sweden's largest dedicated property company made its debut on the Stockholm bourse on Monday, marking an end to the big four banks' unwilling tenure as the country's largest real estate owners.

With property holdings valued at around 25 billion crowns ($3.8 billion), Diligentia becomes easily the largest real estate company in Sweden, outgunning building and property combines Skanska and NCC.
Diligentia is the latest property group to be spun off by Sweden's major banks in a move which they hope will draw a line under a financial crash in the early 1990s.
Shareholders in Wallenberg group banking arm S-E-Banken received an extra payout of one share in Diligentia for every 10 shares held in the bank.

As one property company after the other failed in the wake of a collapse in real estate values, banks were saddled with huge stocks of buildings -- taken over as collateral on bad loans -- which they were neither ready nor willing to manage.

Only state-controlled Nordbanken was spared the worst of the crisis as its bad loans and unwanted property were hived off into companies with solid-sounding names like Securum, Retrieva and Castellum.
But S-E-Banken, Handelsbanken and Swedbank were all left with major real estate holdings, which, under bank legislation, they were not allowed to own.

Recognising the anomalous situation, legislators changed tax rules last autumn to allow banks -- and only banks -- to pay out shares in their property companies to shareholders without attracting a swingeing tax bill.
Swedbank's Tornet and Handelsbanken's Nackebro were disposed of in this way in May and June, respectively, and both have outstripped market expectations.

Diligentia was given a hesitant welcome by Swedish investors on Monday. Its shares opened at 82 crowns but a combination of a weak bourse and a recoil in property shares after a protracted rally sent it back to 79 crowns as investors cashed in on their windfall.
Even so, Diligentia is undervalued, analysts say. With an estimated value of 25 billion crowns, the portfolio should be worth something like 475 crowns per share.

A depressed market and the the sector's dubious history rule out a share price anywhere near these levels but an investment in Diligentia still has plenty of potential if the company's listed counterparts are anything to go by, analysts say.
The Tornet share has appreciated by 28 percent since its May 7 launch date and Nackebro has gained 20 percent since June 28, both easily outstripping the rest of the market.

Sweden's fifth-largest bank, Foreningsbanken, has yet to announce a timetable for the disposal of its real estate unit Mandamus but has said it plans to sell properties at home and abroad to a value of 3.5 billion crowns by the end of 1998.
